author: konop
cardQuote: To actually get the data they are going to mine, people have to actually use the thing. This is where I think color will fail... plus they spell colour wrong!
quote: To actually get the data they are going to mine, people have to actually use the thing. This is where I think color will fail... plus they spell colour wrong! (sent from Canada)
storyTitle: At least now we know why Color really got that funding
outcome: Shut down at the end of 2012 after its $41M launch failed to find users.
outcomeDetail: Color launched in March 2011 with $41 million in funding and a photo-sharing app built around proximity and social graphs. The app was widely panned, the company pivoted and reportedly sold its team to Apple, and Color shut the app down at the end of 2012.
note: konop saw the fatal loop: Color's data-mining model needed a mass of users, and the app never gave people a reason to join. The company burned through its record seed round in under two years.

author: Hisoka
cardQuote: Noone will care, and noone will use it. If it won't help you get laid, or boost your ego, it'll be useless.
quote: Noone will care, and noone will use it. If it won't help you get laid, or boost your ego, it'll be useless. We human beings are not rational.
storyTitle: Google Reveals Its Stealth Social Project, Google+
outcome: Consumer Google+ shut down in April 2019.
outcomeDetail: Google+ launched in June 2011 as Google's answer to Facebook. It never built a durable user base; Google announced the consumer shutdown in October 2018 after a data exposure, and the service closed in April 2019.
note: "Noone will care, and noone will use it" was the whole story: Google could force the product into its ecosystem but could not make people post. Google+ outlived the prediction by years, but never became a social network.

author: medman77
cardQuote: The company is all hot air. They have a board full of retired military figure heads that have no experience in medical devices or retail services.
quote: The company is all hot air. They have a board full of retired military figure heads that have no experience in medical devices or retail services. Additionally, they do not have any products to show. Look at their patents. They are all very general and broad. There has been NO FDA CLEARANCE for anything they are doing, which raises legal questions. Speaking of legal, search for lawsuits they are involved in. Their core technology is not even theirs. They stole it from someone else.
storyTitle: Theranos
outcome: Dissolved in September 2018 after fraud charges.
outcomeDetail: Theranos raised hundreds of millions on claims its devices could run hundreds of tests on a finger prick. The Wall Street Journal exposed the technology in October 2015, regulators banned Elizabeth Holmes from operating labs, and the company dissolved in September 2018; Holmes was convicted of fraud in 2022.
note: medman77 looked at the board, the empty product shelf, and the missing FDA clearances and called Theranos "all hot air" five years before the WSJ exposé. The theft allegation was never the point; the core technology did not work as advertised.

author: untog
cardQuote: I can't find any info on their site about subscription pricing (always a red flag) but this whole thing seems absurdly stupid.
quote:
Yes, but they're also out $400 on every customer. And those customers can now very easily switch to a different juice provider without losing any "investment" they made in hardware.

I can't find any info on their site about subscription pricing (always a red flag) but this whole thing seems absurdly stupid. I'd be amazed if they managed to scale this in such a way that shipping refrigerated juice to individual customers is more affordable than people picking it up in the store/receiving it with their normal grocery order.
storyTitle: Juicero May Be Feeling the Squeeze
outcomeDetail: Juicero sold a $400-$700 internet-connected juicer with proprietary produce packs. After Bloomberg showed the packs could be squeezed by hand, sales collapsed; the company cut prices and staff, then announced it was shutting down on September 1, 2017.
note: untog saw that the hardware subsidy and refrigerated juice delivery could not scale. Five months later, Juicero was gone.

author: ceejayoz
cardQuote: It's not. Article says they're planning on burning VC money and figure out some nebulous "sell data analytics" sort of monetization approach.
quote:
> How is this remotely profitable?

It's not. Article says they're planning on burning VC money and figure out some nebulous "sell data analytics" sort of monetization approach.
storyTitle: MoviePass wants to let you go to the theater once a day for $10 a month
outcome: Shut down in September 2019 after burning through cash.
outcomeDetail: MoviePass cut its price to $9.95 a month in August 2017 and paid theaters full price for every ticket. Losses mounted, the service was repeatedly restricted, parent company Helios and Matheson went bankrupt, and MoviePass shut down on September 14, 2019.
note: The $10 plan was never a business; it was a customer-acquisition stunt funded by investors. ceejayoz called the data-analytics story what it was.

author: pl0x
cardQuote: WeWork is a giant ponzi scheme on the brink of financial collapse. 2008 is happening all over again.
quote: WeWork is a giant ponzi scheme on the brink of financial collapse. 2008 is happening all over again.
storyTitle: WeWork’s CEO Makes Millions as Landlord to WeWork
outcomeDetail: WeWork's 2019 IPO collapsed after its S-1 revealed huge losses and Adam Neumann's conflicts; SoftBank rescued the company, but the pandemic and an office glut sank it. WeWork filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on November 6, 2023.
note: The "ponzi scheme" label was hyperbole, but the structural point—losses funded by ever-new capital and related-party deals—was exactly what broke WeWork.

author: ShawnBird
cardQuote: Google Glass will probably fail (at least the first iteration) but give some data for the next attempt. Then when Apple comes out with iGlasses everyone can act impressed.
quote: I am sure that that is going to be the product that actually takes off. Google Glass will probably fail (at least the first iteration) but give some data for the next attempt. Then when Apple comes out with iGlasses everyone can act impressed.
storyTitle: Google Glass
outcomeDetail: Google Glass launched to developers in 2013 at $1,500. Privacy backlash, social awkwardness, and limited utility kept it out of the mainstream; Google stopped selling the Explorer edition in January 2015 and later refocused Glass on enterprise, which it discontinued in 2023.
note: ShawnBird predicted the first iteration would fail and hand its lessons to the next attempt. Google halted Explorer sales in 2015 and later retreated to enterprise-only Glass.

author: minimaxir
cardQuote: Meerkat is treading water, and due to the higher burn rate of 1-to-many video, even with $11M funding it will die out quickly.
quote:
Meerkat is treading water, and due to the higher burn rate of 1-to-many video, even with $11M funding it will die out quickly.

Periscope is doing better but not enough to justify a $100M acquisition.

The spike is due to the piracy of the Mayweather boxing fight: if piracy becomes the sole use case and gets even more attention from content providers, both die immediately from the resulting lawsuits.
storyTitle: Evan Spiegel Reveals Plan to Turn Snapchat into a Real Business
outcomeDetail: Meerkat launched in February 2015 and briefly owned live mobile broadcasting. Twitter cut off its social graph and launched Periscope, and Meerkat never found a durable audience; it was pulled from the App Store on September 30, 2016.
note: minimaxir saw that one-to-many video was expensive and that Meerkat's growth was event-driven. It died out within 16 months.

author: suprgeek
cardQuote: The Jawbone up was an unmitigated disaster - should never have been released.
quote:
None of the current generation of the "band" devices are in the finished category. I have tried the Basis B1, Jawbone up and my current device the Fitbit Flex.

The Basis was the most sensor packed bundle of the lot and that is a device with lot of promise - two major issues for me:

- I never got used to the fact that it needs to be in Snug contact with your skin 24/7 for all the sensors to work this can get tricky when you sleep (for example) and the device is on on too tight

- No vibrational alarm A device that senses when you go to sleep does not have a simple mechanism to wake you up smartly - just stupid.

The Jawbone up was an unmitigated disaster - should never have been released.

My current device is the Fitbit which seems to have gotten most of the stuff right, but I still have to tell it when I fall asleep and when I am woken up.
I also have the Aria Scale from fitbit.

As other commenters have echoed, the first device that will make it "totally frictionless" to record all the data will be a blockbuster.

My Ideal fitness device will also have a powerful camera that can take a fast snapshot of any food I eat, use magic algorithms to find a match to stuff known foodstuff (by using Image matching against a database of known foods) and automatically give me the calories and micro-nutirents of everything that I Eat/Drink.

Then we combine all this data with services such as WellnessFX & their Blood Markers...

Then we integrate implantable "micro-labs" that sample your blood 24/7...

Then we add in genetic data from 23andMe...
storyTitle: Why I threw away three Jawbone UPs, sold my Fitbit Flex and deinstalled Human
outcomeDetail: Jawbone's UP fitness trackers were plagued by hardware failures and returns. The company raised hundreds of millions but lost the wearables market to Fitbit and Apple; it stopped making trackers in 2016 and began liquidation in July 2017.
note: The comment was about a product that "should never have been released"—and Jawbone's repeated reliability problems were central to its collapse.

author: pkamb
cardQuote: I remember a service that put a physical DVD in an individual DVD player in a warehouse somewhere and streamed it to you. Essentially the same thing as this? Looks like it was shut down.
quote: I remember a service that put a physical DVD in an individual DVD player in a warehouse somewhere and streamed it to you. Essentially the same thing as this? Looks like it was shut down.
storyTitle: Appeals court upholds legality of Aereo’s “tiny antennas” scheme
outcome: Shut down in November 2014 after losing at the Supreme Court.
outcomeDetail: Aereo rented tiny antennas to stream broadcast TV over the internet without paying retransmission fees. The Supreme Court ruled in June 2014 that this violated copyright, and Aereo suspended service and filed for bankruptcy that November.
note: pkamb pointed to a near-identical service that had already been shut down. Aereo's legal theory lost 6-3 at the Supreme Court.

author: skore
cardQuote: But if your concept is to break boundaries, have no model for actual growth apart from ripping other companies off and not even a chance of making amends (apart from maybe changing the law in every country of the world, which won't happen), I guess it's very clear you're doomed to failure.
quote:
If anybody read that quote and then went on to do something like Grooveshark, I'd guess it's safe to say they need to adjust their reality compass. It may be OK to push the boundaries in certain areas, grow big and make amends later. But if your concept is to break boundaries, have no model for actual growth apart from ripping other companies off and not even a chance of making amends (apart from maybe changing the law in every country of the world, which won't happen), I guess it's very clear you're doomed to failure.

I don't like what the record industry is doing in general these days, but grooveshark was always very obviously shady if not illegal.
storyTitle: All Major Labels Are Suing Grooveshark
outcome: Shut down in May 2015 after losing a copyright case.
outcomeDetail: Grooveshark launched in 2006 and streamed user-uploaded music without licenses. Major labels sued, a court found the company and its founders liable for copyright infringement in 2014, and Grooveshark shut down on May 1, 2015 as part of a settlement.
note: skore called the model "doomed to failure" because it had no lawful path to scale. The labels eventually proved it in court.

author: scottlocklin
cardQuote: This is either going to end up dominating the food delivery business (unlikely, but possible) or present yet another case study in Silicon Valley delusions.
quote:
This is either going to end up dominating the food delivery business (unlikely, but possible) or present yet another case study in Silicon Valley delusions.

It's entirely possible, easy even, to automate the pizza making process. You can go to the grocery store and purchase frozen pizzas which have never been touched by human hands. Exactly none of them are made by industrial robots. Industrial robots cost more than a pizza assembly line does, and they don't do anything that the line can't do. The only way this could make sense is if they could get them robots to make lots of other things, but, well "best of luck with that." At $18 for a pizza, they obviously aren't saving enough money on labor to pass this on to consumers.
storyTitle: Zume, a new startup trying to make a more profitable pizza through robotics
outcome: Exited pizza in 2020 and shut down in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Zume raised hundreds of millions from SoftBank for robot-made pizza, but its economics never worked. It laid off most of its staff in January 2020, pivoted to packaging, and shut down in June 2023.
note: scottlocklin saw that industrial robots cost more than the pizza line they replaced and that $18 pizzas were not saving enough on labor. The "case study in Silicon Valley delusions" line landed.

author: nikcub
cardQuote: As was pointed out when Secret launched by many, the model can never be secret.
quote:
Anonymous application that users install on their phones that identify them, using their personal email addresses and real-life social networks turns out to not be so anonymous.

mindblown.gif

As was pointed out when Secret launched by many, the model can never be secret. It has been interesting to watch the company feel their way around in the dark to a conclusion that anybody in infosec or who understands security/anonymity could have told them before they launched.
storyTitle: Your Anonymous Posts to Secret Aren’t Anonymous After All
outcomeDetail: Secret launched in 2014 as an anonymous social app for friends. A de-anonymization flaw, bullying, and flagging growth led co-founder David Byttow to shut it down in April 2015, less than two years after launch.
note: nikcub said the model "can never be secret" because it was built on phone contacts and identity. The anonymity promise was the product's fatal contradiction.

author: thrownaway954
cardQuote: It kills me to think that they don't realize that their business is a fad and like all fads they fizzle out. couple with the fact that i'm almost certain they will share their information with anyone who is willing to pay them for it and you've got yourself a sinking ship.
quote: It kills me to think that they don't realize that their business is a fad and like all fads they fizzle out. couple with the fact that i'm almost certain they will share their information with anyone who is willing to pay them for it and you've got yourself a sinking ship.
storyTitle: 23andMe lays off 100 people as DNA test sales decline
outcomeDetail: 23andMe's DNA-test sales peaked and then fell; the company cut staff in 2020 and 2024, suffered a major data breach, and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in March 2025. Its assets were sold to Regeneron.
note: The comment called consumer DNA testing a fad and a "sinking ship" five years before the bankruptcy. Sales did fizzle, and the data-privacy liability never went away.

author: microdrum
cardQuote: There aren't any network effects a la Uber and Lyft because the scooter doesn't come to you, you go to it. And the scooters do not go fast/long enough to stitch different catchement areas together. Every sign points to commodification here.
quote: There aren't any network effects a la Uber and Lyft because the scooter doesn't come to you, you go to it. And the scooters do not go fast/long enough to stitch different catchement areas together. Every sign points to commodification here. The way car and bike rentals are commodified. The economics leaks in many places: 1) people buy their own scooters 2) with rising scooter usage, scooters get way cheaper (see 1) 3) multiple competitors bid down rental prices 4) people figure theft/secondary part market out 5) a scooter inventory uniting meta app (a la Kayak) takes all the margin 6) turns out teenagers were only bird hunting as a novelty, gotta pay expensive 25 year olds to do it So many issues. It's easier to see a world where electric scooters are neat novelties for tourists sometimes (as long as it's warm! with no kids! and no rain! and we're going more than 0.7 but less than 2 miles! and my wife doesn't say they're dangerous!) than a world where any one of these companies is a serious $1b technology company. I mean: doesn't it just feel natural?: these are little novelty tourist scoot rental companies.
storyTitle: Scooter startup Bird is seeking a $2B valuation
outcomeDetail: Bird launched dockless e-scooters in 2017 and raced Lime for market share. Heavy losses, city regulation, and a SPAC collapse led Bird Global to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2023; its assets were sold in 2024.
note: microdrum saw no network effect, no moat, and a commodification race that would cap every scooter company below the $1B mark. Bird filed for bankruptcy five years later.

author: marshray
cardQuote: Waving around the terms FDIC- and SIPC-insured in a way that implies that it means something to the end consumer is, IMHO, the sign of a scammer.
quote:
> However, if the exchange itself goes under you SOL.

Either your deposits are federally protected from failure of the institution, or not.

It's as ridiculous as me telling my credit card issuers that their loans to me are federally protected because I have an FDIC bank account.

Nobody's worried about some bank going under, we're worried about the risk of trusting our money with a crypto exchange when so many have been Ponzi schemes.

Waving around the terms FDIC- and SIPC-insured in a way that implies that it means something to the end consumer is, IMHO, the sign of a scammer.
storyTitle: FDIC issues cease and desist letter to FTX US [pdf]
outcome: Filed for bankruptcy in November 2022; founder convicted of fraud.
outcomeDetail: FTX collapsed in November 2022 after a run on deposits revealed billions in missing customer funds. It filed for Chapter 11 on November 11, 2022, and Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted of fraud and sentenced to 25 years in prison.
note: marshray read the FDIC fight as a tell: a crypto exchange hinting that customer deposits were insured was "the sign of a scammer." Three months later, FTX proved him right.

author: kangnkodos
cardQuote: I think it's a good rule of thumb to assume that anyone who guarantees returns greater than the historical return of the S&P 500 is a ponzi scheme.
quote:
I think it's a good rule of thumb to assume that anyone who guarantees returns greater than the historical return of the S&P 500 is a ponzi scheme.

I don't know of a single reputable bank, hedge fund or publicly traded company that does that.

A huge number of places do have high returns from time to time. But any reputable firm points out that past returns do not guarantee future results. No reputable firm guarantees returns that high in the future.

The key is the guarantee.

Anyone who GUARANTEES returns that high in the future is suspect, and therefore must be more transparent than usual in order to clear the bar. The article indicates that Celsius was less transparent than usual in describing exactly how they made their high returns.
storyTitle: The biggest crypto lending company is a ponzi scheme
outcome: Filed for Chapter 11 in July 2022; founder convicted.
outcomeDetail: Celsius promised high yields on crypto deposits and lent the money into risky, related-party bets. It froze withdrawals in June 2022 and filed for Chapter 11 on July 13, 2022; founder Alex Mashinsky later pleaded guilty to fraud and was sentenced to 12 years.
note: kangnkodos's rule—guaranteed returns above the S&P 500 are a Ponzi tell—fit Celsius's opaque yield machine. The company went bankrupt seven months later.

author: clavalle
cardQuote: Yik Yak is going to have to fundamentally change to have a future. It is the most useless app I've downloaded on my phone.
quote:
Yik Yak is going to have to fundamentally change to have a future.

It is the most useless app I've downloaded on my phone. Every time I've ever tried to use it I felt like I had completely wasted my time.

There are a lot of users but each new user doesn't bring that much to the experience. In fact, beyond a certain number they just increase the likelyhood that something negative is going to further pollute the community space.

So, not only is it worse that useless, its main metric is actually functioning backward compared to any other social media app.

There are a lot of smart people throwing a lot of money at this thing. I'd love for one of them to explain the reason because I just don't see it.

Edit: I thought of the perfect metaphor just now talking with my friend who'd never heard of Yik Yak and trying to describe it: It is like reading your local bathroom stall. A half a billion dollars worth of stall walls.
storyTitle: The inside story of Yik Yak
outcomeDetail: Yik Yak launched in 2013 and became a campus hit, but anonymous bullying and moderation problems scared off advertisers and users. The company cut staff in 2016 and shut down in April 2017; Square bought its engineering team.
note: clavalle's "half a billion dollars worth of stall walls" line nailed the product's moderation problem: more users made the feed worse, not better.

author: I_HALF_CATS
cardQuote: Print circulation numbers multiplied by 10, traffic multiplied by 4-10 times and dodgy hiring practices. All these corporate shenanigans, to me, add up to the largest house of cards in the media world.
quote:
AUTHOR NOTE:
I discovered news.Y from traffic statistics to an earlier version of this article. The article remains a "work in progress" but has been significantly updated.

http://vicemediakit.com redirects to https://medium.com/thoughts-on-media/vice-media-kit-warning-... 

If self-posting is banned I'll delete this. Otherwise I'll try to answer any questions.

SUMMARY:
Print circulation numbers multiplied by 10, traffic multiplied by 4-10 times and dodgy hiring practices. All these corporate shenanigans, to me, add up to the largest house of cards in the media world.

ABOUT ME:
After getting my M.Arch I realized I was in a unique position to write a book on Vice Media. I wrote it because I believe click-fraud and anti-competitive practices are drowning out the honest players in the media world.
storyTitle: Is Vice Media's 4.5B valuation an illusion? (Updated)
outcomeDetail: Vice grew from a punk magazine into a digital-media unicorn valued at $5.7 billion, but its revenue never justified the valuation. It filed for Chapter 11 in May 2023 and was sold to a consortium of lenders.
note: The comment's "largest house of cards in the media world" line was self-interested, but the inflated traffic and valuation were real. Vice collapsed seven years later.

author: cylinder
cardQuote: In addition, their $20/hr price is unsustainable and will have to go up once they demand profitability. Two week wait times to book a cleaning may appear to indicate heavy demand, but it also indicates poor planning and resource management.
quote:
And what about the fact that Homejoy got caught trying to buy Yelp reviews? Even still, their Yelp reviews are quite poor in many big markets (Yelp reviews are a major driver in this business)? In addition, their $20/hr price is unsustainable and will have to go up once they demand profitability. Two week wait times to book a cleaning may appear to indicate heavy demand, but it also indicates poor planning and resource management.

Apparently all that matters anymore is how much VC money you can raise, not the underlying business. "Journalism" in this sector is so incredibly lazy.
storyTitle: Homejoy (YC S10) Raises $38M as It Looks to Expand Beyond Home Cleaning
outcomeDetail: Homejoy expanded on-demand home cleaning to dozens of cities at discounted hourly rates. Worker-classification lawsuits, poor unit economics, and the difficulty of retaining cleaners led it to shut down on July 31, 2015.
note: cylinder saw that the discounted hourly price could not cover cleaner pay and growth, and that VC money was masking the underlying business. Homejoy ran out of time and money 19 months later.

author: ekanes
cardQuote: I expect the product will fail because Google sucks at social stuff, but in principle more competition is good, and unless a company competes unfairly through a monopoly (and they don't have one for email or social networking.)
quote:
With this move, Google is declaring war on a host of web companies that are heretofore thriving and collaborating and making tons of money.

From the perspective of those other companies they are indeed "declaring war" and it's all very dramatic... but for actual users, this is just another company competing for their attention by providing a better service.

I expect the product will fail because Google sucks at social stuff, but in principle more competition is good, and unless a company competes unfairly through a monopoly (and they don't have one for email or social networking.)
storyTitle: Google Buzz
outcomeDetail: Google Buzz launched in February 2010 as a social layer inside Gmail. A privacy backlash over auto-following contacts hurt adoption, and Google announced in October 2011 that it would shut Buzz down; it was discontinued in December 2011.
note: ekanes's one-line verdict—"Google sucks at social stuff"—predicted a decade of Google social failures, starting with Buzz. The product lasted less than two years.

author: mgkimsal
cardQuote: This notion that "the market says $499 price points are what tablets should be priced at" is stupid. $499 is what iPads will sell at - no one else has yet demonstrated that a $499 is viable for any other tablet than the iPad.
quote:
It's not necessarily all or nothing.

Certainly they've already spent quite a lot - trade shows, etc - and have the geek faithful aware of the tablet already. It'd be much easier for me to evangelize this at a lower price point.

A $299 price point would rock. "Correct, it doesn't do as much as an iPad, but it's also not as expensive."

This notion that "the market says $499 price points are what tablets should be priced at" is stupid. $499 is what iPads will sell at - no one else has yet demonstrated that a $499 is viable for any other tablet than the iPad. I will say it's foolish to keep trying this late in the game. If a company as big as HP isn't willing to do what it takes to get these in to peoples' hands (which may include selling below cost), there's little hope this will be a viable competitor.
storyTitle: HP TouchPad: Shipping July 1
outcome: Discontinued in August 2011, seven weeks after launch.
outcomeDetail: HP launched the TouchPad on July 1, 2011, priced to match the iPad. It sold poorly; HP killed the device and its webOS hardware on August 18, 2011, and cleared inventory in a $99 fire sale.
note: mgkimsal called matching the iPad's $499 price "foolish" and said HP needed to sell below cost. HP ended up doing exactly that—at $99, after killing the product.
